cues.text: Docker versus Virtual Machines.
A virtual machine emulates a whole computer and boots its own operating system.
A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel.
VMs give stronger isolation; containers are far lighter and start in about a second.
In this lesson: overview, how containers isolate, side by side, when to use which, a request walked through step by step, the key takeaways, and interview practice.
Overview.
Both solve "it works on my machine": they package an app with everything it needs so it runs the same everywhere.
They differ in where the line between app and machine is drawn.
A VM virtualizes hardware.
A hypervisor splits one physical server into several virtual ones, and each runs a complete guest OS.
A container virtualizes the operating system.
All containers share the host's Linux kernel; the kernel just gives each one its own view of the system.
How containers isolate.
Namespaces give a process its own view: its own process list (pid), network interfaces (net), filesystem mounts (mnt), hostname (uts), and users (user).
cgroups limit what it can use: CPU, memory, disk I/O, number of processes.
The image's layers are stacked with a union filesystem (overlayfs), plus a thin writable layer per container.
There is no second kernel: a container is a normal Linux process with restrictions.
That is why it starts in about a second and why one server can run hundreds.
Side by side.
Size: a VM image carries a full OS, typically gigabytes.
A container image carries only the app and its libraries, typically tens to hundreds of megabytes.
Start time: a VM boots an OS, often tens of seconds to minutes.
A container starts a process, usually under a second.
Density: tens of VMs per server versus hundreds of containers.
Isolation: a VM has its own kernel, so a kernel exploit in one guest does not reach the others.
Containers share one kernel, so a kernel bug can affect all of them.
OS choice: a VM can run Windows on a Linux host.
A Linux container needs a Linux kernel.
When to use which.
VMs: a different OS, strong isolation between untrusted tenants, legacy apps that expect a full machine.
Containers: microservices, the same image from laptop to CI to production, fast scaling.
Both, very often: cloud containers usually run inside VMs, and Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS runs a small Linux VM to provide the kernel.
Lightweight VMs like Firecracker (AWS Lambda, Fargate) combine VM-level isolation with near-container start times.
Let's follow one request through the design: Shipping a Python web app with Docker.
Step 1.
The Dockerfile is the recipe: start from a small Python image, install dependencies, copy the code, set the start command.
Step 2.
docker build runs each instruction and saves the result as a layer.
Layers are cached, so changing only your code rebuilds only the last layers.
Step 3.
docker push uploads only the layers the Registry does not have yet.
Step 4.
On the server, the Docker Engine pulls the image, again skipping layers it already has.
Step 5.
docker run asks the kernel for new namespaces and a cgroup with limits, then starts the process inside them.
Step 6.
The container is just a Linux process on the shared kernel.
It starts in about a second, and inside it sees only itself.
Step 7.
The same app in a VM: the Hypervisor (KVM, ESXi) gives it virtual hardware, and a full Guest OS per VM has to boot before the app can start.
Step 8.
Each VM carries its own kernel: heavier, but a kernel bug in one guest does not reach the others.
Key takeaways.
1: A VM virtualizes hardware and boots its own OS; a container is an isolated process on a shared kernel.
2: Namespaces give a container its own view; cgroups limit what it can use.
3: Containers are megabytes and start in about a second; VMs are gigabytes and take far longer.
4: VMs isolate better: every guest has its own kernel.
5: Images are layered and cached: order a Dockerfile from least to most often changed.
6: In the cloud, containers usually run inside VMs.
Interview practice.
I'll ask a question, then pause so you can answer it in your head, or out loud if the carriage is empty.
Question 1.
Why can't a Linux container run a Windows app natively?
Question 2.
What do layers buy you when 50 images share the same base?
Question 3.
How would you run untrusted user code safely: containers, gVisor, or microVMs?
Question 4.
What happens to a container's files when it is deleted, and how do volumes help?
Question 5.
Why do Kubernetes nodes run in VMs in most clouds?
That's Docker versus Virtual Machines.

URL Shortener.
Turns a long URL into a short code and redirects anyone who opens the code.
It is a classic read-heavy system: one link is created once and opened many times, so the design is mostly about fast lookups.

In this lesson: overview, requirements, capacity estimates, components, data model, key decisions, scaling and failure, a request walked through step by step, the key takeaways, and interview practice.
Overview.
Users submit a long URL and get back a short link like sho.rt/aZ3k9Qx.
Opening that link sends them to the original URL.
Optional extras: custom aliases, expiry dates and click analytics.
The defining property is the read/write ratio.
A link is written once and read many times, often 100 reads per write, so the redirect path is what you optimize.
Requirements.
Functional:
Create a short code for a long URL (optionally a custom alias and an expiry).
Redirect a short code to its URL.
Count clicks per link.
Non-functional:
Redirects must be fast: a few milliseconds inside the service.
Highly available: a broken redirect is a broken link on someone else's page.
Codes must be unique and hard to guess if links are private.
Capacity estimates.
Illustrative numbers, typical for an interview:
100 million new links a month is about 40 writes per second on average.
At 100 reads per write, that is about 4,000 redirects per second, with peaks of maybe 10 times that.
At roughly 500 bytes per row, five years of links (6 billion rows) is about 3 TB, which suits a sharded relational store or a key-value store.
Code length: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion codes, so 7 base62 characters (a–z, A–Z, 0–9) last a very long time.
Components.
Load Balancer: spreads traffic across stateless API servers, so you scale by adding servers.
Shorten API: validates the URL (format, blocklist), gets an ID, stores the mapping.
Key Generator (base62): hands out unique IDs; base62 encoding turns a number into a short, URL-safe code.
Redirect API: the hot path.
Look up, redirect, emit an event, nothing else.
Redis Cache: holds popular codes.
Link traffic is very skewed, so a small hot set serves most redirects.
URL Database: the source of truth, keyed by short code.
Click Event Queue and Analytics Worker: keep analytics off the redirect path so slow counting never delays a redirect.
Stats Store: aggregated counts for dashboards.
Data model.
urls: one row per short link.
shortcode is UNIQUE, which also creates the index every redirect uses.
userid is nullable so anonymous links work.
users: the people who create links.
urldailystats: one row per link per day, primary key (urlid, day).
Counting per day keeps the table small; raw click events stay in the queue or a log store, not in the OLTP database.
Key decisions.
How to generate codes.
A counter encoded in base62 never collides, but is guessable and needs coordination.
Hashing the URL (and truncating) needs collision checks.
Random codes need a uniqueness check on insert.
A common answer: each server reserves a block of IDs (say 1,000 at a time) from a central counter, so there is no per-request coordination.
A 301 (permanent) is cached by browsers, which saves traffic but means later clicks never reach you: no analytics, and you cannot change the target.
A 302 (temporary) sends every click through the service.
Cache-aside with a TTL: read the cache, fall back to the database, then populate the cache.
Links rarely change, so stale entries are rarely a problem.
Async analytics: never count clicks synchronously on the redirect path.
Scaling and failure.
Reads: add Redirect API servers and cache capacity first, then database read replicas.
Storage: shard the URL Database by short code (hash-based) once a single node is not enough.
Hot links: a viral link can overload one cache node.
Replicate hot keys or add a small in-process cache on each server.
Cache stampede: when a popular entry expires, many requests hit the database at once.
Use request coalescing or refresh entries early.
Key Generator as a single point of failure: block reservation means servers keep working through short outages.
Abuse: rate-limit link creation, and scan target URLs for phishing and malware.
Let's follow one request through the design: https://www.example.com/blog/2026/how-we-scaled-our-database-to-a-billion-rows.
Step 1.
User / Browser asks to shorten the URL.
The Load Balancer forwards it to one of the Shorten API servers.
Step 2.
Shorten API validates it: scheme https, host www.example.com, 78 characters.
It would also check the host against a malware blocklist.
Step 3.
Key Generator hands out the next unique ID, and base62 turns it into a 7-character code.
Step 4.
The mapping is stored.
shortcode is UNIQUE, so a duplicate could never be inserted.
Step 5.
The short link goes back to the user.
Step 6.
Later, someone opens https://sho.rt/2cVydGc.
The Load Balancer sends it to a Redirect API server.
Step 7.
In cache?
First the Redis Cache is checked.
This link is new, so it is a miss.
Step 8.
On a miss, the URL Database is read using the unique index on shortcode (a few milliseconds).
Step 9.
The answer is put in Redis Cache with a TTL, so the next visits skip the database.
Step 10.
Redirect API answers with 302 and the browser follows the Location header to the original page.
Step 11.
Without slowing the redirect, a click event goes to the Click Event Queue; the Analytics Worker adds it to the daily count.
Step 12.
The next visitor gets a cache hit: Redis answers in under a millisecond and the database is not touched.
Key takeaways.
1: Give each link a unique ID from a counter and write it in base62: 7 characters cover 3.5 trillion links.
2: Reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1, so optimise the redirect path.
3: Cache hot codes in Redis; the database only sees cache misses.
4: Keep API servers stateless so you can add more behind the load balancer.
5: Count clicks through a queue, never inside the redirect.
6: Hand each server a block of IDs so the counter is not a bottleneck.
Interview practice.
I'll ask a question, then pause so you can answer it in your head, or out loud if the carriage is empty.
Question 1.
How would you support custom aliases without collisions?
Question 2.
How do you make codes unguessable for private links?
Question 3.
What changes if each link must redirect differently by country or device?
Question 4.
How do you delete expired links without slowing down the database?
Question 5.
How would you guarantee a link keeps working if a whole region goes down?
That's URL Shortener.
Next up: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
Instead of granting permissions to each user, you grant them to roles (admin, editor, viewer) and give users roles.
Access checks become "does any of this user's roles include this permission?".
In this lesson: overview, core model, components, where to enforce, key decisions, scaling and failure, a request walked through step by step, the key takeaways, and interview practice.
Overview.
Two different questions are involved, and mixing them up is the most common mistake:
Authentication (authN): who are you?
Answered at login.
Failure is 401 Unauthorized.
Authorization (authZ): what may you do?
Answered on every request.
Failure is 403 Forbidden.
RBAC is a way to answer the second question that stays manageable as users grow: you manage a handful of roles instead of thousands of individual grants.
Core model.
A permission is an action on a resource, written like "invoice:read" or "invoice:approve".
A role is a named set of permissions, like "accountant".
A user has one or more roles.
Their effective permissions are the union of their roles' permissions.
Both links are many-to-many, which is why the database uses two join tables: userroles and rolepermissions.
Principles: deny by default (no matching permission means no access), and least privilege (give each role only what it needs).
Components.
Login Service: authenticates users and issues tokens.
It is the only place that sees passwords.
Users & Roles DB: the source of truth for users, roles, permissions and the links between them.
Issue J W T (roles claim): signs the token (RS256 lets any service verify it with the public key).
API Gateway: checks the token once at the edge, so services do not each re-implement it.
Policy Check: turns roles into permissions for the requested action; can live in the gateway or a shared library.
Protected Service: still checks ownership rules itself (see "Where to enforce").
Audit Log: append-only record of access decisions, required by most compliance standards.
Where to enforce.
Coarse checks ("only editors may call POST /articles") fit well in the gateway.
Fine-grained checks ("editors may edit only their own drafts") need data the gateway does not have, so the service enforces them.
When rules depend on attributes (owner, department, time of day), RBAC alone stops scaling.
That is where ABAC (attribute-based access control) or relationship-based models (like Google Zanzibar) come in; many real systems combine RBAC with a few attribute checks.
Key decisions.
Roles in the token versus looked up per request.
Roles in the J W T avoid a database call on every request, but changes (like removing a role) only take effect when the token expires.
Typical answer: short-lived access tokens (about 5 to 15 minutes) plus refresh tokens, with permissions cached per role.
Permission naming: "resource:action" strings are easy to read, check and audit.
Role design: start with a few broad roles.
Too many fine-grained roles ("role explosion") is as hard to manage as per-user grants.
Revocation: for urgent cases (a fired employee), keep a short denylist of revoked token ids until they expire.
Scaling and failure.
Permission checks run on every request, so cache role  to  permissions in memory; it changes rarely.
If the Identity Provider goes down, existing tokens keep working until they expire, but nobody new can sign in.
Run it highly available.
Signing keys must rotate: publish the public keys (JWKS) so services can pick up new ones without redeploying.
Fail closed: if a permission check cannot be completed, deny the request rather than allow it.
Let's follow one request through the design: editor tries article:delete.
Step 1.
The User signs in through the Client App, which sends the credentials to the Login Service over HTTPS.
Step 2.
The Login Service checks the password against the stored bcrypt hash, then loads the user's roles.
Step 3.
Issue J W T: the roles go into a signed, short-lived token.
Anyone can read the claims; only the Identity Provider can sign them.
Step 4.
The Client App calls the API with the token.
The route needs the permission "article:delete".
Step 5.
Token valid?
The gateway verifies the RS256 signature with the public key for kid "key-2026-10" and checks exp.
Both pass.
Step 6.
Policy Check expands the role into permissions and looks for "article:delete".
Step 7.
Has permission?
No.
The user is signed in, but "editor" does not include "article:delete", so the answer is 403 Forbidden (not 401: signing in again would not help).
Step 8.
Refusals are audited too: they are how you spot misconfigured roles or someone probing the API.
Key takeaways.
1: Authentication asks who you are (401); authorization asks what you may do (403).
2: Grant permissions to roles and roles to users, never permissions to users directly.
3: Deny by default, and give each role only what it needs.
4: Short-lived J W Ts carry roles; a removed role stops working when the token expires.
5: Check coarse rules at the gateway and ownership rules in the service.
6: Audit every decision, refusals included.
Interview practice.
I'll ask a question, then pause so you can answer it in your head, or out loud if the carriage is empty.
Question 1.
A user's role is removed.
How quickly does it take effect, and how would you make it immediate?
Question 2.
How would you let editors edit only their own articles?
Question 3.
How do you support role hierarchies, where admin inherits everything editor has?
Question 4.
Where do you store tokens in a browser, and how do you protect them from XSS and CSRF?
Question 5.
How would multi-tenant RBAC work, where roles differ per organization?
That's Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
Next up: Uber Surge Pricing & Artificial Scarcity.
Uber Surge Pricing & Artificial Scarcity.
Surge pricing raises the price where riders outnumber free drivers, to pull more drivers in.
Because the price reacts to supply, drivers can fake a shortage by going offline together: artificial scarcity.
A robust design prices from smoothed, sanity-checked supply and locks the price the rider sees.
In this lesson: overview, the problem: artificial scarcity, fixes, components, key decisions, scaling and failure, a request walked through step by step, the key takeaways, and interview practice.
Overview.
A ride app is a marketplace with two sides.
When riders in one area outnumber free drivers, waits get long.
Surge pricing raises the price there, which does two things: some riders wait or choose another option, and drivers nearby head over.
Supply and demand meet again.
The area unit matters.
Uber divides cities into hexagons with H3, its open-source grid.
Hexagons are used because every neighbour is the same distance away, which makes "this cell and its neighbours" easy to compute.
The problem: artificial scarcity.
The price is a function of supply, so whoever controls supply controls the price.
News reports have described drivers at some airports switching off the app together.
The map shows no free cars, the price surges, and the drivers switch back on to take the higher fares.
That is artificial scarcity: the shortage is fake, the price is real.
Riders overpay, and the honest signal the system depends on is corrupted.
The same weakness applies to any price driven by live supply, like flash sales and ticketing.
Fixes.
Smooth the signal.
Never price from one snapshot.
Average supply over a window of minutes and blend in neighbouring hexagons.
A sudden dip that lasts two minutes barely moves a 10-minute average.
Detect coordination.
Normal churn is spread out; a coordinated logout is many drivers, one hexagon, one minute.
Leave those drop-offs out of supply and review the accounts.
Lock the price.
The rider sees one upfront price when they request, valid for a short time, so a manipulated spike a minute later cannot change it.
Forecast and nudge.
Flights landing, concerts ending and rain are predictable.
Use forecasts and heatmaps to bring drivers in before the spike, so there is less shortage to exploit.
Change the incentive.
Pay drivers bonuses tied to an area and time window rather than the live multiplier at the moment of acceptance, so logging off to spike the price stops paying.
Components.
API Gateway: authenticates the apps and turns their updates into events.
Kafka (location events): a durable, ordered stream; hundreds of thousands of drivers sending updates every few seconds is a high-volume write stream that a database should not take directly.
Stream Processor: a streaming job (Flink is common) that keeps windowed counts per hexagon in memory.
Supply & Demand per H3 Cell: the current counts, kept in a fast key-value store and also written to surgesnapshots for analysis.
Coordinated Drop-off?: rules or a model over driverstatusevents.
Pricing Service: reads smoothed counts and forecasts, and returns a multiplier per hexagon.
Locked Upfront Quote: a short-lived quote stored with an expiry, honoured at booking.
Key decisions.
Hexagon size: smaller cells react to local demand but have few drivers each, so the counts are noisy and easier to manipulate.
Larger cells are stable but blunt.
Smoothing across neighbours gets some of both.
Window length: a longer window resists manipulation but reacts more slowly to real spikes, like a stadium emptying.
Forecasts help cover the gap.
Fairness and caps: many places limit surge during emergencies; the pricing service needs a cap per region.
Explainability: store the inputs for every multiplier (surgesnapshots), so you can answer "why was this ride ₹600?".
Scaling and failure.
Partition the Kafka topic by hexagon (or region), so one processor owns the counts for a set of cells and no coordination is needed.
If the stream lags, prices go stale.
Fail safe: fall back to 1 times  or the last good value with a short expiry, never to an extreme multiplier.
Late and duplicate GPS events happen on mobile networks; count by event time, deduplicate by (driver, timestamp), and tolerate a little lateness.
Hot cells (airports, stadiums) get far more events; keep enough processor partitions for them.
Let's follow one request through the design: 8 riders, 14 drivers usually, 12 went offline.
Step 1.
Every Driver App reports its location and status every few seconds through the API Gateway.
In the last two minutes, 12 of the 14 drivers in this hexagon switched to offline.
Step 2.
Riders opening the Rider App count as demand in the same hexagon: 8 are waiting.
Step 3.
Events land in Kafka, and the Stream Processor keeps running counts per H3 hexagon.
Step 4.
A naive design would price from this snapshot: 8 riders ÷ 2 drivers gives 2.2 times .
That is the number a coordinated logout tries to trigger.
Step 5.
Coordinated drop-off?
Yes: 12 drivers (86% of the hexagon) left within two minutes.
Their drop is not treated as a real shortage, and the accounts go to review.
Step 6.
Smooth over Time & Space: average the trusted supply over the last 10 minutes, and blend in the neighbouring hexagons, so a short dip barely moves it.
Step 7.
The Pricing Service applies the rule to the smoothed supply: 1.0 times  instead of 2.2 times .
Step 8.
The rider gets a Locked Upfront Quote: whatever happens to supply in the next two minutes, this price holds.
Step 9.
With a normal price, Dispatch / Matching simply offers the trip to the nearest driver.
Key takeaways.
1: Surge compares riders asking with free drivers, per H3 hexagon.
2: A price driven by live supply can be gamed: a coordinated logout fakes a shortage.
3: Smooth supply over minutes and neighbouring hexagons, never one snapshot.
4: Flag many drivers going offline in one place at once.
5: Lock the rider's price when they request.
6: Forecast demand and bring drivers in before the spike.
Interview practice.
I'll ask a question, then pause so you can answer it in your head, or out loud if the carriage is empty.
Question 1.
How would you detect a coordinated logout that is spread over 10 minutes instead of 1?
Question 2.
How do you choose the hexagon size and the smoothing window?
Question 3.
What happens to prices if the stream processor is 2 minutes behind?
Question 4.
How would you design surge so that it stays fair during an emergency?
Question 5.
How would you prevent riders from gaming it, for example by requesting from a cheaper neighbouring hexagon?
That's Uber Surge Pricing & Artificial Scarcity.

Twitter Timeline & Search.
Users post tweets, read a home timeline built from everyone they follow, and search.

Reads dwarf writes, so the home timeline is precomputed: each new tweet is pushed into followers' timelines in memory (fan-out on write), except for celebrities, whose tweets are merged in when a timeline is read.
In this lesson: overview, requirements, capacity estimates, components, key decisions, scaling and failure, a request walked through step by step, the key takeaways, and interview practice.
Overview.
Two timelines matter:
The user timeline: one person's own tweets.
Easy: a query on tweets by userid.
The home timeline: tweets from everyone you follow, newest first.
Hard: it combines hundreds of people, and it is the most-read page in the product.
Computing the home timeline on every read (fan-out on read) means querying everyone you follow each time.
Instead, this design does the work once per tweet (fan-out on write) and keeps every active user's home timeline ready in memory.
Requirements.
In scope:
A user posts a tweet; followers get push notifications and emails.
A user views their user timeline and their home timeline.
A user searches by keyword.
High availability.
Out of scope: the firehose and other streams, visibility rules (hidden replies and retweets), analytics.
Capacity estimates.
Assumptions from the System Design Primer:
100 million active users; 500 million tweets a day (15 billion a month).
Each tweet fans out to 10 followers on average: 5 billion deliveries a day.
250 billion timeline reads and 10 billion searches a month.
Which works out to:
About 6,000 tweets per second written, 60,000 fan-out deliveries per second.
About 100,000 timeline reads per second and 4,000 searches per second.
About 10 KB per tweet with media: 150 TB of new content a month, 5.4 PB in three years.
Handy rule: 400 requests per second  about  1 billion requests per month.
Components.
Web Server: a reverse proxy in front of the API servers (TLS, routing, compression).
Write API, Read API, Search API: stateless servers for the three paths, scaled separately.
Fan Out Service: turns one tweet into N home-timeline writes, in the background.
User Graph Service: who follows whom, cached in memory.
Timeline Service: builds the response from cached ids plus multigets.
Memory Cache (Redis): each home timeline is a list of (tweetid, userid, meta), 8 + 8 + 1 bytes per entry.
SQL Database: the source of truth for tweets and users.
Object Store: photos and video.
Search Cluster: an inverted index (Lucene-style), kept in memory for low latency.
Notification Service: sends pushes and emails off a queue.
Key decisions.
Fan-out on write versus on read.
On write: reads are one cache lookup, but each tweet costs O(followers) writes.
On read: tweets are cheap, every timeline read is expensive.
Twitter-scale read traffic favours writing.
The celebrity problem.
Fanning out a tweet to tens of millions of followers takes minutes and floods the cache.
Skip fan-out above a threshold and merge those accounts' recent tweets in at read time: a hybrid.
What to keep in memory.
Only the newest few hundred entries per timeline, and only for users active in the last 30 days.
An inactive user's timeline is rebuilt from SQL when they come back.
Ids, not tweets, in the timeline lists: tiny entries, and edits or deletes only touch the Tweet Info Service.
REST for public APIs, RPC between internal services.
Scaling and failure.
The Fan Out Service is the obvious bottleneck.
Slow fan-out can also make a reply appear before the tweet it answers; re-ordering by timestamp at serve time hides that.
The SQL Database will not keep up with 6,000 writes per second plus cache misses on one primary: add read replicas, then federation (split by function), sharding (split by user), and denormalization.
Some data fits NoSQL better, for example timelines and the social graph.
Keep the Search Cluster's index in memory; queries scatter to every shard, so one slow shard slows every search.
Benchmark, profile, fix the worst bottleneck, repeat: scaling is iterative.
Let's follow one request through the design: @devnews (12,000 followers) posts a tweet.
Step 1.
@devnews posts a tweet.
The Client sends it to the Web Server (a reverse proxy), which forwards it to the Write API.
Step 2.
The Write API saves the tweet to the author's own timeline in the SQL Database.
That is the user timeline: the author's own tweets, in order.
Step 3.
Media goes to the Object Store, not the database: a tweet row stays small, and photos and videos are served from cheap blob storage (usually behind a CDN).
Step 4.
The Write API hands the tweet to the Fan Out Service, which asks the User Graph Service who follows the author.
The follower lists live in the Memory Cache.
Step 5.
Fan-out on write: the tweet id is pushed onto the home timeline of each of the 12,000 followers in the Memory Cache.
It is O(n): 12,000 followers means 12,000 inserts, and each list is trimmed to its newest 800.
Step 6.
The tweet is added to the Search Cluster so keyword searches can find it within seconds.
Step 7.
Notifications go out through the Notification Service, which works off a queue so a slow push or email provider never delays the post.
Step 8.
The author gets a response as soon as the tweet is saved; fan-out, indexing and notifications carry on in the background.
Key takeaways.
1: The home timeline is read far more than tweets are written, so build it ahead of time: fan out on write.
2: Fan-out is O(followers): fine for most users, far too slow for celebrities.
3: Skip fan-out for accounts with millions of followers and merge their tweets in at read time.
4: Keep timelines in memory, only the newest few hundred tweets, and only for active users.
5: Store tweets in SQL for the user timeline; serve home timelines from the cache.
6: Push notifications and indexing through queues so posting stays fast.
Interview practice.
I'll ask a question, then pause so you can answer it in your head, or out loud if the carriage is empty.
Question 1.
Where exactly would you put the celebrity threshold, and how would you measure it?
Question 2.
A user unfollows someone.
How do their tweets leave the home timeline?
Question 3.
How do you rebuild the timeline of a user who has been away for a year?
Question 4.
How would you rank the timeline instead of sorting it by time?
Question 5.
How would you make a tweet searchable within a few seconds of posting?
That's Twitter Timeline & Search.

Web Crawler & Search.
A crawler keeps a priority queue of links, fetches the most important page, skips it if a near-identical page was already crawled, and otherwise queues it for indexing.
Search reads only the reverse index (word  to  pages) and the stored titles and snippets.
In this lesson: overview, requirements, capacity estimates, components, key decisions, scaling and failure, a request walked through step by step, the key takeaways, and interview practice.
Overview.
Two systems share the data:
The crawler: runs all the time, turning links into indexed pages.
It is write-heavy and must never get stuck in a loop.
Search: answers user queries from the index.
It is read-heavy and must be fast.
The web is a graph full of cycles and copies (mirrors, URL parameters, printer-friendly pages), so most of the design is about deciding what not to crawl.
Requirements.
In scope:
Crawl a list of URLs, building a reverse index of words to pages and a static title and snippet per page.
A user searches and sees relevant pages with titles and snippets.
High availability.
Out of scope: search analytics, personalized results, PageRank.
Capacity estimates.
Assumptions from the System Design Primer:
1 billion links, refreshed about weekly: 4 billion crawls a month.
500 KB stored per page; 100 billion searches a month.
Which works out to:
2 PB of page content a month, 72 PB in three years.
About 1,600 page writes per second.
About 40,000 searches per second.
Components.
linkstocrawl: the frontier, a priority queue of URLs (NoSQL, or a sorted set in Redis).
crawledlinks: every crawled URL with its signature and last-crawl time.
Crawler Service: many workers pulling from the frontier, polite per site.
Reverse Index Queue and Document Queue: decouple crawling from indexing.
Reverse Index Service: maintains word  to  list of pages (posting lists), sharded by word.
Document Service: generates static titles and snippets.
Query API: parses the query (strip markup, split terms, fix typos, normalize case, build a boolean query), looks up the index, ranks, and adds snippets.
Key decisions.
Duplicate URLs: with a billion links, deduplicate with MapReduce (keep URLs whose count is 1) or a Bloom filter in front of the frontier.
Duplicate content: compare page signatures (simhash, or Jaccard and cosine similarity over word sets).
Near-duplicates, not just exact copies, must match.
Freshness: store a last-crawled timestamp; refresh about weekly, more often for popular or frequently changing pages.
Learn each page's change rate over time.
Politeness: obey robots.txt and limit requests per site, or you will be blocked (and you will hurt small sites).
Static snippets: generated once at crawl time, so search never touches page content.
Scaling and failure.
Shard the frontier and assign each site to one worker group, which makes per-site rate limits easy.
DNS lookups add up at this scale: cache them in the crawler.
Popular queries repeat a lot: cache their results in front of the Query API.
Shard the Reverse Index by word or by document; a query fans out to shards and merges the results.
A crawler worker crashing mid-page just leaves the link in linkstocrawl; jobs on the queues retry.
Let's follow one request through the design: https://blog.example.org/raft-explained.
Step 1.
The Crawler Service takes the highest-priority link from linkstocrawl.
Priorities start from site popularity, so important pages are crawled first.
Step 2.
It fetches the page from The Web (respecting robots.txt and a per-site rate limit), then computes a signature from its content.
Step 3.
Similar page crawled?
No signature in crawledlinks is close, so this is new content.
Step 4.
Two jobs are queued: one for the Reverse Index Service (which words appear on which pages) and one for the Document Service (a static title and snippet).
Queues let crawling run at its own pace.
Step 5.
The link moves from linkstocrawl to crawledlinks with its signature, and the page's own links are added to linkstocrawl for later.
Step 6.
The Reverse Index Service adds the page to each word's posting list in the Reverse Index; the Document Service stores its title and snippet.
Step 7.
Later, someone searches for "raft consensus".
The Query API parses the query, finds matching pages in the Reverse Index, ranks them, and fetches titles and snippets.
Key takeaways.
1: Crawl from a priority queue (the frontier), seeded by site popularity.
2: Detect duplicate content with page signatures, or the crawler loops and wastes work.
3: Lower a duplicate's priority instead of crawling it again.
4: Hand indexing and snippet generation to queues so crawling never waits on them.
5: A reverse index maps each word to the pages containing it; search reads only that.
6: Re-crawl on a schedule (about weekly), more often for pages that change often.

Question 1.
How would you detect that two pages are the same article with different ads around it?
Question 2.
How do you avoid crawler traps, such as infinite calendar pages?
Question 3.
How would you decide which pages to re-crawl every hour?
Question 4.
